recent_posts.title: More Practicality, Less Theory • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: Community poll data from enterprise architects reveals that stakeholder buy-in is often misidentified as the core problem with architecture frameworks. In reality, the difficulty lies in translating frameworks into practical, daily work. Only 1% of respondents struggle to understand framework concepts, while 52% want clearer practical examples rather than more training or theory. The post argues that architecture fails when relevance isn't made visible early enough, and introduces the Enterprise Architecture Implementation Wheel as a TOGAF-based, pragmatic four-stage approach (Document, Define, Execute, Control) to bridge the gap between theory and practice.

recent_posts.title: A Scrapbook of Past Projects • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: Enterprise Architecture often devolves into a fragmented scrapbook of past projects. The TOGAF Architecture Repository offers a conceptual framework — not a tool — for treating architecture as a coherent, reusable body of knowledge. Key components include the Architecture Landscape (Strategic, Segment, and Capability levels), Reference and Standards Libraries, a Governance Repository, and Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs vs SBBs). The post emphasizes that the repository should be selectively curated, actively used, and kept minimal, enabling architecture to be institutional rather than episodic.

recent_posts.title: Starting Your Career in EA • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: Practical career advice for those entering Enterprise Architecture, emphasizing that EA is fundamentally about understanding the business rather than mastering frameworks or tools. Key guidance includes: prioritizing business understanding over technology obsession, acting as a bridge between business and IT rather than a compliance gatekeeper, building credibility through relationships and outcomes rather than polished diagrams, and developing durable skills like critical thinking, storytelling, and facilitation. The post stresses patience and influence as core career assets, noting that tools and frameworks will change but these foundational skills endure.

recent_posts.title: Architecture Beyond Domains • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: Traditional Enterprise Architecture frameworks like TOGAF divide work into four domains (business, data, application, technology), creating silos that fragment responsibility and limit holistic thinking. A more effective approach views architecture through organizational scope levels—Enterprise, Segment, and Solution Architects—where each role maintains an organization-wide perspective at different granularities. The Enterprise Architecture Implementation Wheel offers a modern alternative that centers architecture as a guiding force through continuous cycles of documenting, defining, executing, and controlling, rather than partitioning by domain. This shift enables architects to contribute across all concerns while maintaining strategic coherence and alignment.

recent_posts.title: Risk Management (2
recent_posts.summary: Explains how to perform risk assessment in enterprise architecture using TOGAF's Risk Management technique. Covers initial risk assessment during Phases E and F, measuring impact and frequency on 1-5 scales, combining these factors into risk classifications (critical, high, moderate, low), and visualizing risks using Risk Heat Maps. Details risk monitoring during Phases G and H, calculating risk scores using the formula Risk = Impact × Frequency, and plotting risks on heat maps to prioritize mitigation efforts based on organizational risk tolerance.

recent_posts.title: Risk Management (1
recent_posts.summary: Risk Management is integrated throughout TOGAF's Architecture Development Method (ADM), specifically in phases A, E, F, G, and H. The technique involves identifying, classifying, and mitigating risks across time, cost, and scope dimensions. Initial risks are assessed and documented, then mitigated to become residual risks. Organizations categorize risks by impact and frequency, visualize them in heat maps, and track them through implementation. The approach differs from comprehensive Enterprise Risk Management, focusing primarily on architecture project risks rather than broader organizational concerns.

recent_posts.title: Architecting with AI • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: AI enhances rather than replaces traditional enterprise architecture frameworks like TOGAF's Architecture Development Method (ADM). The integration spans all ADM phases: from AI-assisted capability assessment and scenario modeling in early phases, to automated process discovery and data profiling in business and information architecture, to intelligent migration planning and continuous governance monitoring. AI acts as a force multiplier, providing speed, automation, and data-driven insights while preserving human judgment and strategic thinking essential to effective enterprise architecture.

recent_posts.title: Architecture Across Ages • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: Enterprise Architecture shares fundamental principles with ancient Greek architecture: balance, clarity, purpose, and adaptability. Both disciplines emphasize proportional design, phased construction, standardization, and stakeholder engagement. Modern EA practitioners can learn from Greek builders' approach to site analysis, iterative development, and community-centered design. The TOGAF ADM mirrors ancient construction phases, while reference architectures serve as contemporary equivalents to classical proportional standards. Success in both fields requires balancing stability with flexibility and building for long-term evolution rather than static monuments.

recent_posts.title: EA: The Missing Puzzle Piece • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: Enterprise Architecture serves as the critical connecting element that aligns strategy, processes, data, and technology within organizations. Rather than being an optional refinement, EA provides the big-picture view needed to prevent fragmented initiatives and siloed systems. The discipline has evolved from early IT frameworks like TOGAF to encompass full enterprise scope, addressing business capabilities, data models, and governance. Organizations lacking EA typically exhibit signs like failed strategy execution, data silos, expensive integrations, and shadow IT emergence. Modern EA practices are adaptive and contextual, focusing on enabling action through artifacts like capability models, value streams, and roadmaps rather than rigid documentation. Success requires executive sponsorship, starting small with targeted pain points, and consistently tying deliverables to business decisions.

recent_posts.title: Certified Experience • EAWheel
recent_posts.summary: The Open Group offers experience-based certifications through the Open CA Program, which differs from traditional knowledge-based certifications like TOGAF by requiring candidates to demonstrate real-world architectural experience. The program covers four disciplines (Digital, Business, Solution, and Enterprise Architecture) across three certification levels (Certified, Master Certified, and Distinguished). The certification process involves three phases: milestone applications covering professional communication and development plus experience profiles, a detailed certification application explaining architectural decisions, and a peer review board defense. Only 41 architects worldwide hold the Master Certified Enterprise Architecture specialization, making it highly exclusive.
